content.intro: Past Simple is the tense for things that are over. You did them, they finished, and usually you know when.
content.explanation:
Use Past Simple for an action that started and finished in the past. The time is either stated (yesterday, last week, in 2020) or already clear to both people. Regular verbs add -ed. Irregular verbs have their own second form (V2) that has to be learned: go → went, see → saw, buy → bought.

The form is the same for every subject: I went, she went, they went. The only thing that changes is what happens in negatives and questions, where did takes the tense and the main verb goes back to its base form.
usage: Completed actions at a definite time in the past
A sequence of past events, in order
Past habits and states that are no longer true
Past events in a story or a report

examples.text: I visited London last summer.
She studied medicine for six years.
We woke up, had breakfast and left.
He didn't call me back.
Did you enjoy the film?

common_mistakes.why: After didn't, use the base form. Did already carries the past.
After did, use the base form.
With a finished past time like yesterday, use Past Simple, not Present Perfect.

In a question, did comes before the subject.

content.intro: Present Simple is the tense for things that are generally true: habits, routines and facts.
content.explanation:
Use Present Simple for what happens regularly or what is always true, not for what is happening at this exact moment. The form is the base verb, except with he, she and it, which add -s or -es.

Negatives and questions use do or does, and once do/does appears, the main verb goes back to its base form: she works → she doesn't work.

formulas.label: Affirmative
formulas.pattern: I / you / we / they + V1  ·  he / she / it + V1 + s

usage: Facts and things that are always true
Feelings and opinions with stative verbs

Water boils at 100 degrees.
The train leaves at six.
She doesn't eat meat.

Does already carries the -s, so the main verb is the base form.
With he, she and it, the question word is does.
Know is a stative verb and is not used in the continuous.

content.intro: Present Continuous is for what is happening now, or around now — not for what is always true.
content.explanation:
Use Present Continuous for an action in progress at this moment, or for a temporary situation around this period of time. It is built from am/is/are plus the -ing form.

It is also used for fixed future arrangements: I'm meeting Ali tomorrow. Some verbs — know, believe, want, need, belong — describe states rather than actions and are not normally used in the continuous.

examples.text: I'm studying for an exam.
Look — it's raining.
Prices are rising.
We're meeting at six tomorrow.

common_mistakes.why: The continuous needs the verb be as well as the -ing form.
Know is a stative verb, so it takes the simple form.
After am/is/are, the verb takes -ing.
Short verbs ending in one vowel + one consonant double the consonant.

questions.explanation: At the moment signals the continuous.

content.intro: Present Perfect links the past to now. The action happened before, but what matters is the situation today.
content.explanation:
Use Present Perfect when the past action still matters now: an experience you have had, a change that has happened, or something that started in the past and is still going on. It is built from have/has plus the third form of the verb (V3, the past participle).

The key rule: do not use it with a finished past time. If you say when it happened — yesterday, last year, in 2020 — English switches to Past Simple.
usage: A past action with a result you can see now
Something that started in the past and continues

examples.text: I have been to Japan.
examples.note: An experience. We do not say when.

examples.text: She has lost her keys.
examples.note: The result is now: she cannot get in.

examples.text: We have lived here for ten years.
examples.note: Started in the past, still true.

examples.text: Have you finished yet?

common_mistakes.why: Yesterday is finished time, so Past Simple.
Present Perfect takes V3 (gone), not V2 (went).

common_mistakes.right: I have been here since Monday.
common_mistakes.why: Something continuing from the past takes Present Perfect.
In a question, has comes before the subject.

questions.explanation: Started in the past, still true.

questions.explanation: Last year is finished time: use Past Simple.

content.intro: Past Continuous shows an action in the middle of happening at a moment in the past.
content.explanation:
Use Past Continuous for an action that was already going on at a past moment. It very often meets a Past Simple action: the long action is the background, the short action interrupts it.

It is built from was/were plus the -ing form. Was goes with I, he, she and it; were goes with you, we and they.

formulas.label: With Past Simple
examples: I was cooking when the phone rang.

usage: An action in progress at a past moment
A long action interrupted by a short one
Two actions happening at the same time
Setting the scene in a story

examples.text: At nine o'clock I was still working.
The phone rang while I was cooking.
examples.note: Short action interrupts a long one.

examples.text: She was reading and he was cooking.
examples.note: Two actions at the same time.

examples.text: The sun was shining and the birds were singing.

common_mistakes.why: After was/were the verb takes -ing.
They takes were, not was.

common_mistakes.wrong: While I cooked, the phone was ringing.
common_mistakes.right: While I was cooking, the phone rang.
common_mistakes.why: The long background action takes the continuous; the short one takes Past Simple.
Know is stative and is not used in the continuous.

questions.explanation: The long action takes the continuous.

content.intro: The is the definite article: we use it when both people know exactly which one is meant.
content.explanation:
Use the when the thing is already identified — because it was mentioned before, because the situation makes it obvious, or because there is only one of it.

The does not change for singular, plural, countable or uncountable: the book, the books, the water. What decides it is not the noun but whether the listener already knows which one.

formulas.label: Second mention
examples: I bought a book. The book was excellent.

formulas.label: Made specific
examples: the man in the blue coat

usage: Something there is only one of
Groups of islands, rivers, seas and some countries

The sun rose at six.

common_mistakes.why: Talking about something in general takes no article.

content.intro: A and an introduce one thing for the first time, when it does not matter which one.
content.explanation:
Use a or an with a singular countable noun that the listener does not yet know about. The choice between them is about sound, not spelling: a before a consonant sound, an before a vowel sound.

That is why it is an hour (the h is silent) but a university (it starts with a 'y' sound).
usage: Introducing something for the first time
One of many, when it does not matter which

content.intro: First Conditional talks about a real possibility in the future and what will happen if it comes true.
content.explanation:
Use First Conditional when the situation might genuinely happen. The if-clause takes the present simple — even though it is about the future — and the result clause takes will.

The two halves can go in either order. When the if-clause comes first it is followed by a comma; when it comes second there is no comma.

formulas.label: Standard
formulas.pattern: If + present simple, will + base verb
examples: If it rains, I will stay home.

formulas.label: Reversed
formulas.pattern: will + base verb + if + present simple
examples: I will stay home if it rains.

formulas.label: Negative
formulas.pattern: If + present simple, won't + base verb
examples: If you don't hurry, we won't catch the train.

usage: Cause and effect that has not happened yet

examples.text: If I finish early, I'll call you.
If you touch that, you'll burn yourself.

I'll help you if you ask.
examples.note: No comma when if comes second.

common_mistakes.right: If you come, I will be happy.
common_mistakes.why: Present simple in the if-clause, will in the result.

common_mistakes.wrong: If she studies she will pass.
common_mistakes.right: If she studies, she will pass.
common_mistakes.why: When the if-clause comes first, it takes a comma.

common_mistakes.wrong: Unless you don't hurry, we'll be late.
common_mistakes.right: Unless you hurry, we'll be late.
common_mistakes.why: Unless already means if not, so do not add another negative.

content.intro: Second Conditional imagines something that is not true now, and says what would happen if it were.
content.explanation:
Use Second Conditional for an unreal or very unlikely present or future situation. The if-clause takes the past simple — not because it is about the past, but because English uses a past form to signal distance from reality — and the result clause takes would.

With the verb be, formal English uses were for every subject: if I were you, if he were here.

formulas.label: Standard
formulas.pattern: If + past simple, would + base verb
examples: If I had a car, I would drive to work.

formulas.label: With be
formulas.pattern: If + subject + were, would + base verb
examples: If I were you, I would apologise.

formulas.label: Negative
formulas.pattern: If + didn't + base verb, wouldn't + base verb
examples: If I didn't work, I wouldn't earn anything.

usage: Giving advice with 'If I were you'

content.intro: The passive puts the action first and the person who does it second — or leaves them out entirely.
content.explanation:
Use the passive when who did something is unknown, obvious or simply not the point. English builds it from the verb be plus the third form of the main verb (V3).

If you do want to name the doer, add by: The bridge was built by the Romans. Most of the time in the passive, you do not.

formulas.label: Affirmative
examples: These cars are made in Japan.

formulas.label: Negative
examples: The office isn't cleaned on Sundays.

formulas.label: Question
examples: Is the report written every week?

formulas.label: With the doer

usage: When the doer is unknown or unimportant

content.intro: Reported speech is how you say what someone else said, without quoting them word for word.
content.explanation:
When you report what someone said, the tense usually moves one step back — this is called backshift — because the moment of speaking is now in the past. Pronouns and time words shift too: I becomes he or she, today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day.

Say and tell are both used, but tell needs a person after it: he told me, not he told that.

formulas.label: Basic
examples: "I am tired." → He said (that) he was tired.

formulas.label: With tell
examples: "I'll call you." → She told me she would call me.

formulas.label: Backshift
formulas.pattern: present → past · past → past perfect · will → would
examples: "I work here." → He said he worked there.

examples.text: "I am busy." → She said she was busy.
"I saw him." → He said he had seen him.
"I'll help." → She said she would help.
He told me he lived in Tashkent.

common_mistakes.right: He told me he was tired.
common_mistakes.why: Say does not take a person directly; tell does.

common_mistakes.right: She said that she was late.
common_mistakes.why: Tell needs a person: she told me that...
The tense shifts back one step after a past reporting verb.

common_mistakes.wrong: She said she will come tomorrow.
common_mistakes.right: She said she would come the next day.
common_mistakes.why: Will becomes would, and tomorrow becomes the next day.

content.intro: A defining relative clause tells you which person or thing is meant. Without it, the sentence does not identify anything.
content.explanation:
A defining relative clause is joined to the noun it describes with who, which, that, whose, where or when. It is essential: remove it and you no longer know which one is being talked about.

It takes no commas. And when the relative pronoun is the object of the clause, it can be dropped altogether: the book (that) I read.

formulas.label: People
examples: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.

formulas.label: Things
examples: The book which won the prize is excellent.

formulas.label: Pronoun dropped
examples: The film we watched was long.

usage: Saying which person or thing you mean
Combining two short sentences into one
Adding essential detail without a new sentence

content.intro: Some verbs are followed by -ing, some by to + verb, and a few change meaning depending on which you choose.
content.explanation:
There is no rule that predicts which verb takes which: the pattern has to be learned with the verb. Enjoy, avoid, finish, mind and suggest take the gerund. Want, decide, hope, promise and agree take the infinitive.

A small group takes both with a real change in meaning. Stop doing means you end the activity; stop to do means you pause in order to do something else. Remember doing is a memory of the past; remember to do is not forgetting a duty.

formulas.label: Verb + gerund
formulas.pattern: enjoy / avoid / finish / mind / suggest + V-ing

formulas.label: Verb + infinitive
formulas.pattern: want / decide / hope / promise + to + V

formulas.label: Change of meaning
examples: I stopped smoking. / I stopped to smoke.

usage: Choosing the right form after a verb
As the subject of a sentence
Where the choice changes the meaning

examples.text: I enjoy cooking.
She decided to move.
He is good at drawing.
I stopped buying coffee.
I stopped to buy coffee.
examples.note: I paused in order to buy it.

common_mistakes.why: Enjoy is always followed by the gerund.

common_mistakes.right: I want to read that book.
common_mistakes.why: Want is always followed by the infinitive.

common_mistakes.wrong: She is good at to swim.
common_mistakes.why: After a preposition, English always uses -ing.

common_mistakes.wrong: I'm looking forward to see you.
common_mistakes.right: I'm looking forward to seeing you.
common_mistakes.why: Here to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

questions.explanation: Stopped in order to buy: infinitive.

payload.sentence: I avoid to eat late.

questions.explanation: Enjoy and avoid take -ing; want and hope take to.

content.intro: Much goes with things you cannot count; many goes with things you can.
content.explanation:
Much is used with uncountable nouns — water, money, time, information — and many with plural countable nouns — bottles, coins, hours, facts.

In positive statements both sound formal, so everyday English usually prefers a lot of, which works with either kind. Much and many are most natural in questions and negatives.

examples.text: How much does it cost?
How many people came?
I don't have much free time.
There were a lot of cars.
examples.note: A lot of in a positive statement.

common_mistakes.why: People is countable, so it takes many.
Money is uncountable, so it takes much.

common_mistakes.wrong: How many informations do you need?
common_mistakes.right: How much information do you need?
common_mistakes.why: Information is uncountable and has no plural.
Cars is plural countable, so too many.

content.intro: A question tag is the short question added to the end of a statement to check or confirm it.
content.explanation:
The tag mirrors the statement and flips it: a positive statement takes a negative tag, a negative statement takes a positive one. The tag reuses the auxiliary from the statement — or do/does/did if there isn't one — and the subject becomes a pronoun.

Intonation changes the meaning: falling, you are confirming something you believe; rising, you are genuinely asking.
usage: Checking something you believe is true

examples.text: It's cold today, isn't it?
You don't drive, do you?
She finished the report, didn't she?
I'm next, aren't I?

common_mistakes.wrong: You are coming, aren't you coming?
common_mistakes.why: The tag is only the auxiliary and a pronoun.
The pronoun must match the subject.
A positive statement takes a negative tag.
English has no amn't; the fixed form is aren't I.

content.intro: Comparatives say that one thing has more of a quality than another.
content.explanation:
Short adjectives add -er: tall → taller, big → bigger, happy → happier. Longer adjectives take more in front: more expensive, more interesting. Either way, the second thing is introduced by than.

A few are irregular and have to be learned: good → better, bad → worse, far → further.

formulas.label: Long adjectives
examples: This is more expensive than that.

formulas.label: Irregular
examples: This one is better than the other.

usage: Expressing degree with much or a bit

examples.text: My brother is older than me.
This book is more interesting than that one.
The weather is getting warmer.
His English is much better now.

common_mistakes.wrong: She is more taller than me.
common_mistakes.why: Use -er or more, never both.

common_mistakes.wrong: This is more cheap than that.
common_mistakes.why: Cheap is short, so it takes -er.
Comparisons take than, not that.
Good is irregular: better.
